demonstrated evidence from proposals and recommendations, and flags matters needing verification. The source material is a dated company
record, not independent confirmation of current registrations, patent status, program status, competitor claims, or technical results. Verify
time-sensitive facts before external use.

1. Executive Summary
Monsters Ink LLC is a Bellevue, Nebraska small business developing software for deterministic, pre-start resource admission and modular
magnetic-assisted suspension hardware. The software line is at laboratory-prototype or earlier stages; the suspension line is at bench-hardware or
concept stage. The supplied record documents no field deployment, vehicle integration test, contract award, government selection, or issued patent.
The strongest near-term commercialization case is Headroom, supported by a working lab prototype, a reported sub-10-millisecond decision time on lab
hardware, and a stated four-resource admission rule. The next meaningful proof point is not another broad claim: it is a demonstration against a
workload and acceptance criteria agreed with a prospective user.
Three distinct opportunities should be kept separate:
1. Headroom: Seek a mission-representative demonstration, with NDRC and Nebraska defense contacts as a proposed C3/NC3-oriented path.
2. Cue-Share: Maintain the existing DIU submission track, subject to program rules and status verification. Submission is not selection, award, or a
tested adapter.
3. [55,8] codec: Package the reproducible verifier and seek technical review and testing on real noisy-channel data. Current results apply to the
documented fault model and test battery, not every possible error pattern.

Other products should advance only when there is an appropriate customer, test opportunity, or funding path. In particular, MAGPIE should not be
marketed with ride, durability, efficiency, or vibration-performance figures: the source states that vehicle testing and controlled performance data are
absent.

Canonical positioning
Monsters Ink develops systems that make bounded decisions before action: software that admits work only when specified resource
headroom is available, and vehicle hardware intended to add magnetic assistance to conventional damping. The software is a lab-stage
prototype; the suspension hardware is at bench stage. Claims are limited to the tests and evidence documented for each product.
“Refusal” is a design principle, not a blanket guarantee that every product prevents every failure. Use product-specific evidence and limitations.

MONSTERS INK LLC
MASTER TECHNICAL PORTFOLIO
VOLUME I: SOVEREIGN FOUNDATION
Canonical portfolio manuscript
Snapshot date: 7 October 2026
Company: Monsters Ink LLC
CAGE: 24VL0
UEI: R9SQEQR51E46
Location: Bellevue, Nebraska
Founder and first-named inventor: Taylor Heller

Document-Control Note
This volume establishes the portfolio’s common technical vocabulary, evidence rules, architecture, product-family boundaries, maturity baseline, and
intellectual-property inventory. It is based solely on the supplied source corpus, whose principal materials are dated 6–7 October 2026. It is not a legal
opinion, an independent audit, a certification, or a representation of field performance.
The most recent Sovereign Whitepaper enumerates eight patent applications; this volume adopts that eight-item list. Earlier materials in the corpus
state seven applications. The application count and exact filing dates should be reconciled against current USPTO records and confirmed with patent
counsel. No application is represented here as granted.
DIU submission materials subject to separate proprietary legends are not reproduced. Statements about submission status are limited to what the
supplied non-submission materials report.

Executive Synthesis
Monsters Ink LLC’s technical portfolio is organized around a common engineering discipline: make decisions before consequential work begins;
refuse when the required condition cannot be established; preserve a reviewable record; and limit each claim to the evidence that supports it.
The portfolio has three principal technical pillars:
A fault-refusing error-control codec. The designated [55,8] codec uses a seven-row binary parity construction over 48 payload positions. Its
formal results cover single-fault repair, refusal of all two-spike faults in the stated model, and refusal of same-sign multi-spike faults. A disclosed
mixed-sign, three-or-more-spike pattern can nevertheless alias to a single-column syndrome. The construction’s proof package is reported to
reproduce using a one-command verifier.
Headroom deterministic admission control. A working laboratory prototype evaluates residual processing-time, memory, power, and cooling
capacity before admitting work. The admission rule is an AND across those resources: insufficient room in any one means refusal. Decisions and
refusals are recorded in an append-only, hash-chained log. Reported decision-time and false-yes results are laboratory measurements, not
independently audited deployment benchmarks.
MAGPIE resonant magnetic suspension. Bench hardware combines magnetic assistance with ordinary damping and is described as using a
resonant lock. The source materials report a bench demonstration of the resonant lock, but no vehicle integration, instrumented ride-performance
results, durability data, or field validation.

The portfolio also includes Members Gate, a labeled-figure admission concept that prevents compensation across labels; Cue-Share, a maritime
cueing-adapter submission based on the Headroom family; a submitted Space Threat Intelligence Synthesis Engine concept; and suspension-related
concepts for a modular cartridge, adjustable/look-ahead controls, and a two-path shock layout.
The strongest evidence currently attaches to the codec’s bounded mathematical claims and laboratory test results. Headroom and the codec are
internally assessed at TRL 4; that assessment does not establish mission deployment or independent certification. MAGPIE remains at bench-prototype
stage. Across the portfolio, the central distinction is between a mechanism demonstrated in a bounded setting and a system validated in its intended
operational environment.

1. Governing Philosophy

 1.1 The refusal standard
The governing principle is:
Do not promise more than the machine can actually do.
In the software portfolio, this principle means that admission is not a default entitlement. Work is admitted only when the specified conditions are
satisfied; otherwise the system refuses and records the decision. In the codec, a decoder repairs only when a syndrome has a unique permitted
interpretation and the proposed repair passes re-verification. In both cases, refusal is a designed outcome—not an exceptional failure path.
This principle is a portfolio-level design doctrine. It does not mean that every product has the same mechanism, proof, or assurance level. The codec’s
theorems do not, by themselves, prove Headroom’s resource measurements correct, certify Members Gate, or establish MAGPIE performance. Each
product must earn its own evidence.

1.2 Measure, decide, record
The software portfolio follows a recurring sequence:
1. Measure or inspect the relevant state.
2. Apply a defined decision rule.
3. Admit, repair, or refuse according to that rule.
4. Record the outcome where the product design calls for an auditable decision history.
5. Retain the boundary of what the rule has and has not established.

For Headroom, the stated inputs are four resource leftovers. For Members Gate, the relevant distinction is the figure’s label. For the codec, the input is a
syndrome derived from the received word. These systems are related by decision discipline, not by an assertion that they share one implementation.

1.3 Evidence before assurance language
Terms such as deterministic, verified, tamper-evident, resonant, and minimal are used only within the scope supported by the source record. A
laboratory result is not a field result. A reproducible verifier is not an external certification. A patent application is not a granted patent. A concept
submission is not a tested product.

2. Evidence Taxonomy
The portfolio uses the following labels. They describe the basis and status of a claim; some may apply together. For example, a result can be PROVED
under a stated model and also REPRODUCIBLE through an available verification artifact.
| Label | Meaning in this volume | |---|---| | PROVED | Supported by a mathematical argument under stated definitions and assumptions. Where
applicable, the source also reports machine checks. “Proved” does not imply external certification or validation of a physical system. | | MEASURED |
Reported as an observed result from a specified test or laboratory setup. Measurement scope, sample size, and test conditions limit the claim. | |
REPRODUCIBLE | The source identifies an artifact or procedure that can be rerun to check a result. Reproducibility does not, on its own, establish
independent replication, operational validity, or absence of implementation error. | | CONDITIONAL | Supported only under named assumptions,
configurations, or environmental conditions. If those conditions do not hold, the claim does not carry over. | | UNESTABLISHED | Asserted, formulated,
or suggested but not sufficiently formalized, measured, or validated in the supplied record. | | DISPROVED | Contradicted by the stated mathematics or
ordinary arithmetic. Such claims are excluded rather than softened into affirmative claims. |
These labels are load-bearing. A CONDITIONAL claim without its condition becomes UNESTABLISHED. A MEASURED result cannot be generalized
beyond its test basis. A DISPROVED statement is not restored by relabeling it.

3. Portfolio Architecture
3.1 Architecture at a glance
The portfolio has three connected but distinct engineering areas:
| Area | Primary function | Current evidence center | |---|---|---| | Integrity and fault refusal | Detect, repair, or refuse specified faults in short payloads |
Formal codec results and a reproducible software test package | | Admission and decision accountability | Decide whether work fits measured
resource headroom; preserve the decision record | Headroom laboratory prototype and reported laboratory measurements | | Magnetic-assisted
suspension | Develop modular suspension hardware for trucks and UGVs | MAGPIE bench hardware and a reported bench resonant-lock
demonstration |

 The broader product family applies these capabilities to labeled data, maritime cueing, space-domain intelligence concepts, and suspension variants.
Those applications have different maturity levels and must not be treated as if they inherit the strongest evidence of another component.

3.2 The [55,8] fault-refusing codec
Designation and dimensions. “[55,8]” is the portfolio’s name for the codec. The supplied construction is explicitly a 55-symbol codeword consisting of
48 payload symbols and 7 parity symbols. This volume does not infer conventional code parameters from the designation.
Construction. The parity matrix (H) is a (7\times48) binary matrix. Its columns are the first 48 qualifying 7-bit masks in the stated ordering: masks with
bit 0 set and Hamming weight at least 2. In the supplied construction, these are the odd masks from 3 through 97, in increments of 2, with rows ordered
least-significant bit first.
The source materials report the following structural properties:
• 48 distinct columns, each of weight at least 2;
• a common row, bit 0, present in every column, so each pair of columns intersects;
• no pair-sum collision among distinct columns, checked over all 1,128 pairs.

For payload (v\in\mathbb{R}^{48}), the parity tail is (t=Hv), and the codeword is ([v;t]\in\mathbb{R}^{55}). For a received word ([v';t']), the syndrome is
(s=Hv'-t').
The decoder accepts a clean word when the syndrome is within its tolerance; proposes a repair only when the syndrome matches exactly one column by
support and uniform value; rechecks the repaired word by recomputing the syndrome; identifies a single parity-axis edit separately; and refuses other
cases. The supplied excerpt does not specify the numerical tolerance value.
Codec claims and evidence
• PROVED: A single spike produces the corresponding column syndrome and is repairable under the decoder’s unique-match rule.
• PROVED: Unequal-magnitude dual spikes cannot alias to a single-column syndrome for a matrix with distinct columns of weight at least 2.
• PROVED: With the stated seven-row construction, dual spikes of any nonzero magnitudes and signs are refused.
• PROVED: With the construction, any two or more spikes of one strict sign cannot alias to a single-column syndrome.
• PROVED: The source presents a lower-bound argument that six rows cannot provide the specified pair-sum-free property for 48 columns of weight
at least 2; seven rows are sufficient in the construction. The portfolio therefore identifies seven rows as minimal for that property.
• MEASURED: The reported battery records a clean roundtrip maximum error of approximately (1.48\times10^{-14}), 48/48 single-fault repairs, 7/7
tail-edit detections, and refusal of all 1,128 equal-magnitude dual-fault pairs tested. It also records 200/200 sampled unequal-magnitude pairs and
200/200 same-sign triples refused.
• REPRODUCIBLE: The source identifies proof_package/verify.py as a one-command verifier, with 11 checks, NumPy only, and an
expected “ALL CHECKS PASSED” result. The canonical implementation is identified as proof_package/source/codec55.py, with the parity
matrix in proof_package/H_matrix.csv.
• DISPROVED as a universal claim: The codec does not refuse every possible multi-fault pattern. A disclosed mixed-sign fault of order three can
alias to a single-column syndrome. The source gives the example of (+1) at masks 11 and 13 and (-1) at mask 9, producing the syndrome of mask
15. Accordingly, “all multi-faults are refused” is not a valid unqualified claim.

The mathematical boundary is part of the canonical specification: dual faults are within the proved refusal result; same-sign multi-spike faults are within
the proved refusal result; adversarial mixed-sign faults of order three or more are not covered by those guarantees.

3.3 Headroom deterministic admission control
Headroom is described as software operating before a new job starts. It measures four resource leftovers on the target machine:
• processing time;
• memory;
• power; and
• cooling.

Each leftover is compared with the job’s requirement plus a safety margin. Admission is a logical AND: all four must have sufficient headroom. A deficit
in any one resource means refusal. The source materials describe refusal as a first-class outcome intended to leave the system without a half-started job
or partial allocation.
Headroom also includes a decision record described as append-only and hash-chained. The intended record covers both admissions and refusals. The
source states that the record is tamper-evident and allows a reviewer to reconstruct decisions without access to raw sensor data.
Evidence status:

 • MEASURED: Laboratory materials report a decision time below (1/100) second and no false yes in the tested lab scenarios.
• PROVED at the mechanism level / CONDITIONAL at deployment scale: The source characterizes the admission rule as deterministic when
applied to measured residual capacity. Whether that mechanism provides the intended guarantee in a deployment depends on the validity,
timeliness, calibration, and integration of the measurements and workload requirements.
• UNESTABLISHED: Mission-representative workload performance, partner integration, and field operation are not established in the supplied
record. The reported laboratory results are not independently audited benchmarks.

3.4 Members Gate and decision-log component
Members Gate extends admission logic to labeled figures. Its defining rule is non-compensation across labels: surplus in one category cannot cover
a deficit in another. The concept is associated with provisional application 64/169,264.
The supplied maturity assessment places Members Gate at TRL 3. Its non-compensation rule is specified, but laboratory prototype integration against
labeled datasets has not been demonstrated in the source record.
The hash-chained decision log is a Headroom component, assessed internally at TRL 4 as part of that prototype. The corpus notes that hash-chaining
itself is a standard pattern; the portfolio’s stated value is its integration with admission decisions and refusals. No claim is made here that a hash chain
alone prevents every form of tampering or compromise.

3.5 MAGPIE resonant magnetic suspension
MAGPIE is the hardware family for magnetic-assisted suspension modules intended for tactical trucks and unmanned ground vehicles. The described
architecture combines magnets with ordinary dampers and includes modular cartridge concepts.
The Sovereign Whitepaper describes a 1.2 MHz resonant lock, gives the resonant-frequency relation (f_r=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})), and characterizes the lock
as GaN-driven and non-contact across dynamic travel. It also identifies a modular swap-in shock cartridge, a two-path shock layout, and adjustable
look-ahead controls.
These are CONDITIONAL technical descriptions tied to the reported bench prototype and its configuration. The corpus reports a bench demonstration of
the resonant lock. It does not provide vehicle integration results, controlled ride measurements, durability data, shock-reduction percentages, efficiency
figures, or vibration metrics. No such performance figures are claimed in this volume.

3.6 Application concepts
Cue-Share is described as a software-only maritime cueing adapter built on the Headroom admission family. Its stated purpose is to triage sensor cues
